text: and hence to weight loss, anti- neoplastic therapy for breast cancer has also been associated with weight gain, sometimes dramatic.1 Weight gain appeared to be more likely in premenopausal women, in those receiving multi- drug regimens, and in those treated for longer periods of time. A study of premenopausal women found that reduced physical ac- tivity may be a contributing factor to the development of this form of weight gain.2 A subsequent small study has suggested that adjuvant regimens based on doxorubicin and cyclophospha- mide, with or without a taxane, may not be associated with sig- nificant weight gain, although patients may undergo unfavoura- ble changes in body-mass composition.3 Weight gain has also been noted after long-term follow-up of paediatric leukaemia pa- tients.4,5 Causes include cranial irradiation and corticosteroid therapy,6 although some have suggested that weight gain de- pends more on inherent characteristics of the patients than the treatment given.7 Concurrent use of corticosteroids may also lead to weight gain. 1.
